newsitem.title: USA: Christopher made little splash as diplomacy chief.
newsitem.headline: Christopher made little splash as diplomacy chief.

text.p: Warren Christopher failed to sparkle in four years as secretary of state, often blamed for the foreign policy failures of the administration he loyally served, and taking little credit for its successes.
Sympathisers felt that Christopher, who resigned on Thursday, at the age of 71, after President Bill Clinton's re-election this week, was more effective than he looked.

The New York Times said in an editorial on Thursday that Christopher brought "maturity, tenacity and reflection" to U.S. foreign policy, safely guiding an inexperienced Clinton through an uncertain post-Cold War era.

But Christopher's tenure will perhaps be remembered for his inability to achieve the goal he pursued above all others -- a deal between Israel and Syria that would have completed what he called the "circle of peace" in the Middle East.
Aides said Christopher might have stayed on, at least for a while, had that been a realistic prospect.
A likeable if not exactly warm figure, Christopher was widely respected at home and abroad for his decency, courtesy and patience.
Sadly for him, those qualities cut little ice in the brutal world of the mid-1990s. Still, he weathered many diplomatic crises and hung on to his job, which at one point seemed threatened.

But, unlike the civic roles he assumed in his past life as an influential Los Angeles lawyer, Christopher as secretary of state failed to leave an unambiguous personal mark on the diplomatic successes achieved on his watch.
And he shares at least some blame for the failures, including a seriously troubled U.S. relationship with China.
His steady, understated, self-effacing manner made him an effective behind-the-scenes negotiator. But the result was that he often let his lieutenants outshine him.

Ambassador Robert Gallucci got most of the credit for the historic 1994 pact under which North Korea agreed to freeze its nuclear programme, while former President Jimmy Carter -- Christopher's former boss -- smoothed the return to Haiti of democratically elected president Jean-Bertrand Aristide.

Western failure to stop the war in Bosnia clouded the administration's foreign policy. Christopher's willingness to take no for an answer from European allies reluctant to get involved surprised even the allies themselves.
When a peace accord was finally struck last year, former Assistant Secretary of State Richard Holbrooke was unquestionably the energy and intellectual force behind it, and dominated the limelight.

President Clinton himself took much of the credit for the administration's successful gamble in backing President Boris Yeltsin in Russia. The stability of Washington-Moscow ties, despite many storms, was a major factor for world peace.
With no issue has Christopher been more directly involved than the Middle East, where he made some 20 shuttle trips in pursuit of peace.

Early this year, U.S. officials thought an Israel-Syria agreement might be within reach. But within weeks, a series of Islamic suicide bombings in Israel killed off that hope. When right-winger Benjamin Netanyahu was elected Israeli prime minister in May, Washington virtually gave up.

Christopher earned his Washington stripes in the Carter administration by helping to negotiate the release of 52 American hostages from Iran in 1981. He received the Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honour.

Out of government service, he was active on problems in U.S. race relations, heading a commission that in 1992 investigated the Los Angeles Police Department after a citizen filmed white officers beating black motorist Rodney King.
Christopher won praise for a strong report that became a blueprint for sweeping reforms.
He then headed President-elect Clinton's transition team after the 1992 election.
Christopher's discretion is legendary, so much so that even his wife has said she often goes for weeks without any idea of what he is working on. Meticulous preparation is another hallmark.
A lawyer to the tips of his elegant shoes and tailored London suits, Christopher was once named as one of America's best-dressed men by People magazine.
He was born Oct. 27, 1925, in Scranton, North Dakota, but grew up in Los Angeles.
He took a law degree at Stanford University, clerked for Supreme Court Justice William Douglas and practised law in Los Angeles before coming to Washington for a government career.
